In 1899, an independent telephone company received a franchise connected to putting telephone infrastructure underground. Tunnel construction began around 1900. The tracks connected with railroad freight houses. In some buildings, they reached directly into basement -level facilities. And this was not one tunnel linking two points. At its height, the network stretched roughly 60 miles beneath downtown Chicago. For decades, freight moved through an underground grid while the city continued above it. Then in July 1959, the trains stopped.

More than three decades after the last freight train ran, Chicago would get a dramatic demonstration of that fact. On April 13, 1992, water from the Chicago River began pouring into the old freight tunnel system. The breach occurred where the tunnel network passed beneath the river near the Kinsey Street area. Once the water entered, it found the legacy of the freight railroad waiting for it. A connected underground pathway through downtown. The same basic quality that had made the system valuable for freight now made it consequential for an entirely different reason. Water spread through the old tunnels and interconnected

The larger point is more important to this story anyway. The freight railroad had been closed for 33 years. Its physical connectivity could still shape what happened in downtown Chicago. The flood did not bring the railroad back. It exposed something more useful for understanding cities. A system can vanish from everyday economic life without vanishing from the physical logic of the place. The tunnel network no longer had trains, customers, or a freight business.
